chunks.text: The Silk Roads were a web of overland trade routes linking China, Central Asia, India, Persia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean. They were ancient by 1200 but entered a spectacular boom between c. 1200 and c. 1450.

Goods rarely traveled the entire length of the Silk Roads with one merchant. Instead they changed hands many times in a relay, passing from Chinese to Central Asian to Persian to European merchants, multiplying in price along the way, so almost no trader covered the whole route.

Because overland caravan transport was slow, dangerous, and expensive, only goods with high value relative to their weight were worth carrying long distances. This is why the Silk Roads carried luxury goods like silk, porcelain, spices, and gems rather than bulk staples like grain.

The main goods carried along the Silk Roads were luxury items: Chinese silk and porcelain, Indian and Southeast Asian spices, Central Asian horses, and precious metals and gems. These were light, compact, and extremely valuable, justifying the cost of the long journey.

One cause of the Silk Roads boom was rising demand. Prosperous, sophisticated societies across Eurasia, including Song and Yuan China, Dar al-Islam, and a reviving Europe, had wealthy elites who craved luxury goods, pulling trade across the continent.

A second cause of the Silk Roads boom was the rise of large stabilizing empires, especially the Mongols, who secured trade routes by punishing bandits and guaranteeing safe passage. This Mongol-provided security is often called the Pax Mongolica, or 'Mongol Peace.'

The Pax Mongolica, or 'Mongol Peace,' refers to the stability and security the Mongol Empire provided across much of Eurasia in the 1200s and 1300s. By uniting vast stretches of the trade routes under one umbrella, it supercharged Silk Roads commerce.

A third cause of the Silk Roads boom was a wave of commercial and transportation innovations, including roadside inns, better camel saddles, and new forms of credit and banking. These tools made long-distance trade safer and more workable.

Caravanserai were roadside inns spaced roughly a day's travel apart along the Silk Roads, where caravans could rest, water their animals, store goods, and trade. They functioned as part motel, part warehouse, and part marketplace, turning a deadly trek into manageable legs.

Improvements in camel saddles allowed the hardy two-humped Bactrian camel to carry heavier loads across deserts where carts and horses failed. Better transport technology was one of the innovations that intensified Silk Roads trade.

The Chinese use of paper money and 'flying cash,' a kind of promissory note, let merchants move value on paper rather than hauling heavy coins. This financial innovation expanded the scale of long-distance trade.

Bills of exchange were documents that allowed a merchant to deposit money in one city and withdraw it in another. Along with banking houses, they let traders finance large deals across thousands of miles without carrying cash through dangerous territory.

Banking houses were institutions that managed credit and money transfers for merchants engaged in long-distance trade. They helped make larger-scale, longer-distance commerce possible along the Silk Roads.
Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China along the Silk Roads in earlier eras, carried by monks and merchants. The routes had long served as channels for the diffusion of religion.

During the period c. 1200–1450, Islam spread along the Silk Roads into Central Asia as Muslim traders established communities in oasis towns. Merchants carried their faith with them and settled in distant trading cities, where their religion took root.

Chinese inventions including papermaking, printing, gunpowder, and the magnetic compass diffused westward across Eurasia along the Silk Roads. The routes transmitted not just products but technologies and know-how.

The Silk Roads also carried disease. The bubonic plague, known as the Black Death, almost certainly spread westward across Eurasia along trade and conquest routes in the 1300s, killing tens of millions and showing the dark side of connectivity.

Trade along the Silk Roads concentrated in great trading cities such as Samarkand and Kashgar, which grew rich and cosmopolitan as hubs where goods, faiths, languages, and peoples mixed. Trade helped build and enrich these cities.

The most world-changing cargo on the Silk Roads was not the silk that named them but the 'invisible cargo': religions, technologies, ideas, and disease. These intangible exchanges reshaped civilizations across Afro-Eurasia.

The Silk Roads carried high-value luxury goods because overland transport was expensive, while sea routes such as the Indian Ocean could carry heavier bulk goods more cheaply. Confusing the two undermines comparisons of the major trade networks.

Silk Roads trade intensified between 1200 and 1450 due to several causes: rising elite demand (economic), the security of large empires like the Mongols (political), and commercial and transport innovations such as caravanserai and bills of exchange (technological and institutional).

The Silk Roads linked the economies of distant civilizations, spread technologies across Eurasia, built cosmopolitan cities, and allowed disease to devastate the whole network, making them an early example of the deep pattern of globalization. Connection brought wealth, cultural richness, and vulnerability together.
